title: Connexions de Gauss-Manin et équations de Picard-Fuchs. Opération de Cartier : copies de tapuscrit annoté (s.d.), tiré à part (1981), notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting. f: X → S is a smooth morphism of (smooth) complex-analytic spaces. ω is a closed holomorphic relative 1-form on X/S. a and b are two sections of f such that for every s, a(s) and b(s) lie in the same connected component of the fibre X_s.

Step 1 (moving paths). Locally on S one can choose a piecewise-differentiable path C_s: [0,1] → X_s from a(s) to b(s) that depends continuously on s. The path is compact and f is locally a product, so it can be lifted and deformed.

Step 2 (holomorphy). Set I(s) = ∫_{C_s} ω_s = ∫_{a(s)}^{b(s)} ω_s. Because ω is relatively closed, it is locally relatively exact, ω|U = d_{X/S}φ. Cover the path by such U and chain the local primitives, as the bracketed remark does in the case where a(s0) and b(s0) are close enough to share one U. Then I(s) is locally a sum of terms φ(b(s)) − φ(a(s)), so I is holomorphic in s.

Step 3 (period ambiguity). Changing the path to C'_s = C_s + Z_s, with Z_s a continuous family of 1-cycles, gives I'(s) = I(s) + ∫_{Z_s} ω_s. So the incomplete integral is defined only modulo periods.

Step 4 (the operator). Take a formal expression μ = Σ_i D_i ∫_{a}^{b} ω_i, with ω_i closed relative 1-forms and D_i differential operators on S. Applied to the incomplete integrals, its ambiguity is Σ D_i ∫_{Z_s} ω_{i,s}.

Continuation on the next page. If this ambiguity vanishes for every continuous family of cycles, μ is called a (generalized, system-type) Picard–Fuchs equation on X/S. Then μ(a,b) is a well-defined holomorphic function on S. It satisfies the cocycle rule μ(a,b) + μ(b,c) = μ(a,c). Grothendieck then looks for an infinitesimal (de Rham / Gauss–Manin) criterion for μ to be Picard–Fuchs.

Purpose. This is the analytic, transcendental version of the construction sketched on the previous page. There, sections of a group G are sent by the logarithmic derivative g^{-1}dg into Z^1 of a de Rham-type complex. They are then composed with a differential operator factored through stratified modules, with the margin query 'spécial à car. 0 ?'.

Together these pages are a general construction of the Manin map (Manin 1963, 'theorem of the kernel'). Picard–Fuchs operators kill periods. Applied to abelian integrals with variable endpoints, they give a homomorphism from sections, i.e. the Mordell–Weil group of the relative Albanese / generalized Jacobian, to holomorphic or algebraic functions on S.

Grothendieck's set-up is broader than Manin's abelian-scheme setting in four ways:
- it allows arbitrary smooth, not necessarily proper, X/S;
- it uses closed rather than merely holomorphic-differential forms;
- it allows systems of operators D_i acting on several forms at once;
- the cocycle property replaces the group law.
errors: Holomorphy argument: the bracket treats only the case a(s0), b(s0) close enough to share one chart U with ω|U = dφ. In general one must chain primitives along a cover of the path. This is routine but unstated here.
Existence of a continuously varying path C_s needs local liftability of paths. This is fine for submersions locally on S, but it should be noted, since f is not assumed proper.

The definition of a Picard–Fuchs expression quantifies over 'all continuous families of cycles'. Without properness the local system of H_1 need not be locally constant in an obvious way. The well-definedness claim implicitly needs the cycles to be deformable locally on S.
Not an error but a gap: the word 'holomorphe' added for ω is needed. Mere closed smooth relative forms would not give holomorphic I(s).

ideas.what: Holomorphic dependence on parameters of incomplete abelian integrals ∫_{a(s)}^{b(s)} ω_s along sections, via local relative primitives.
ideas.modern_name: Variation of relative periods / Gauss–Manin for relative cohomology H^1(X_s,{a(s),b(s)})
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical (Picard, Fuchs); modern relative Gauss–Manin formalism by Katz–Oda / Deligne

ideas.what: Applying a Picard–Fuchs operator (one annihilating all periods) to an integral with moving endpoints gives a well-defined function, additive in the endpoints (μ(a,b) + μ(b,c) = μ(a,c)).
ideas.modern_name: Manin map / Manin's homomorphism (theorem of the kernel); inhomogeneous Picard–Fuchs equations
ideas.usually_credited_to: Yu. I. Manin 1963 (Mordell over function fields); revisited by Coleman 1990, Chai 1991, Buium (δ-characters), Bertrand

ideas.what: Generalized Picard–Fuchs 'equation' as a finite family (D_i, ω_i) of operators acting on several relative closed 1-forms, defined by the vanishing of Σ D_i ∫_Z ω_i on all cycle families.
ideas.modern_name: Element of the kernel of D_S-module map from ⊕ D_S⊗ω_i to the relative de Rham D-module (Gauss–Manin system)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Katz, Manin; D-module viewpoint of Gauss–Manin (Bernstein, Kashiwara)

missed.claim: Grothendieck sets up the Manin map (Picard–Fuchs operator applied to incomplete abelian integrals between sections) for arbitrary smooth families and closed relative 1-forms, not just abelian schemes. He pairs it with an algebraic version via the logarithmic derivative g^{-1}dg and stratified modules on the previous page, and asks whether it is special to characteristic 0. This anticipates the algebraic reformulations of Manin's kernel theorem by Coleman/Chai and Buium's differential characters, and characteristic-p analogues (Voloch, Buium).

missed.why_it_might_matter_today: The Manin map's rigorous algebraic foundation was only clarified around 1990, after Coleman found gaps in Manin's proof. A ~1972 Grothendieck treatment via stratified modules and log-derivatives, for non-proper families, would be an unrecorded early algebraization of it.

missed.claim: He seeks an infinitesimal criterion (in terms of forms and the Gauss–Manin connection rather than global cycles) for μ to be Picard–Fuchs, and asks whether the construction is special to characteristic 0. Neither is resolved on these pages.

missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Characteristic-p Manin maps (via Cartier operator / p-curvature) are a live topic in function-field diophantine geometry. The dossier itself pairs this material with the Cartier operation.

deep.surprise_reason: The mathematics on this page itself is classical: holomorphy of incomplete integrals and their dependence on paths modulo periods. Its interest lies in being the start of a general, Grothendieck-style construction of the Manin map, which is not documented as Grothendieck's work. That construction is not new as a result (Manin 1963), so the surprise is moderate.
